by car, with a walk on Rocky Neck

A minister’s wife from Sterling, Massachusetts, Mellen came into Fitz Henry Lane’s world after her brother-in-law took the Universalist pulpit in Gloucester in 1855. By the middle of the decade she was working beside Lane, with free use of his drawings and at times his canvases…

The museum owns Theresa Bernstein’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester in Blue⟦1⟧ (1925), Nell Blaine’s ⟦2⟧Wharf Studio, Gloucester⟦3⟧ (1958) and the archive of the Folly Cove Designers; the Rocky Neck Art Colony also credits it with Martha Walter’s ⟦4⟧Rocky Neck Store and My Studio⟦5⟧ (1920). Ask at the desk which are on view.

In the summer of 1923 Jo Nivison painted ⟦0⟧Church Towers, Gloucester⟦1⟧, a head-on view of this church’s twin towers. It was the summer she and Edward Hopper painted together here, and she encouraged him to take up watercolor. We have not found the painting in a public collection.

Bernstein first came to Gloucester in 1916. She and the painter William Meyerowitz stayed here after their marriage in 1919, and in 1924 bought a house on Mount Pleasant Avenue in East Gloucester (a private home), where they hosted friends including Milton Avery. Both helped found the North Shore Arts Association.

A Philadelphia painter trained under William Merritt Chase, Walter had joined the Gloucester colony by 1913 and kept a studio and gallery on Rocky Neck from the later 1910s into the 1920s. The building is now a gallery.
In 1924 Sally Michel rented the studio next to Milton Avery’s here. They married in 1926, and her work supported the family while he painted.

Blaine rented studios on Rocky Neck in 1954 and 1958; the Whitney’s ⟦0⟧Harbor and Green Cloth, II⟦1⟧ dates from the second summer. From 1974 until her death she summered in East Gloucester. The marker is placed on the avenue; the studio addresses are not published.
Walter’s entries at the Pennsylvania Academy in 1915 included a crowded beach at Bass Rocks; Philadelphia critics praised the Gloucester picture. Parking along Atlantic Road is limited.
Bernstein was still painting this beach around 1980, when she was about ninety: the Brooklyn Museum owns ⟦0⟧Rabbits, Good Harbor Beach, Gloucester⟦1⟧. Summer parking is by fee.

The children’s author of ⟦0⟧Mike Mulligan and His Steam Shovel⟦1⟧ taught block printing to her neighbors here and in 1941 founded the Folly Cove Designers, who printed textiles by hand until 1969. Their blocks, fabrics and records are at the Cape Ann Museum.
a downtown walk, then a drive
Hopper came to Gloucester in 1912 with his friend Leon Kroll, and again in the summers of 1923, 1924, 1926 and 1928, mostly painting houses in watercolor. Twelve of his subjects can still be found.
Start here: the museum has the most Hopper context in town, and its docent walks cover the downtown houses.
The church on Church Street. The watercolor is at the Princeton University Art Museum.
A tall yellow Italianate house just up Western Avenue from Stacy Boulevard. The watercolor is at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
On his first visit, in 1912, Hopper painted the fishermen’s houses of the Fort, Gloucester’s Italian neighborhood.
The Second Empire house at the corner of Main and Prospect Streets. The watercolor is at the National Gallery of Art.
Hopper painted the church’s towers from a distance, from about 15–17 Mount Vernon Street; in the same summer Jo Nivison painted them head-on.
An oil, at the Cincinnati Art Museum

The rail yard by the station gave Hopper ⟦0⟧Freight Cars, Gloucester⟦1⟧, with the steeple of St. Ann’s Church behind the cars; the box factory on Cleveland Street has been torn down. The station is the end of the walk, with trains back to Boston.
The Brooklyn Museum bought this watercolor after its 1923 show. The house was part of Augustus Wonson’s estate.
Hopper’s 1912 oil of the harbor was painted from the ground above Cripple Cove. The marker is the cove; the exact spot is not recorded.
The point at the end of Good Harbor Beach. The marker is the beach.

In August 2026 Christopher Rothko gave the museum his father’s ⟦0⟧Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts)⟦1⟧ of 1934, the first Rothko in its collection. It shows the salt-fish sheds of the Reed and Gamage wharfs near Smith Cove, painted from Banner Hill.

Avery painted the crowd watching the total solar eclipse of 1932 at Good Harbor. Two years later the friends met here daily: Edith Rothko remembered that they would “go swimming and play handball,” and Rothko painted the game.
Avery first summered in Gloucester in 1921; in 1926 he and the sculptor Leonard Craske rented cottages here, the one record of where he stayed. His ⟦0⟧Gloucester Dawn⟦1⟧ of about 1921 is at Vassar.

Smith Cove was the center of Gloucester’s gill-net fishing. Rothko painted its wharfs again and again in 1934: the Reed and Gamage salt-fish sheds with a water tank on the roof, and rows of fish flakes covered with white cloths to keep the sun off the fillets; fishermen among the gill-net reels on a wharf…

The ridge above Smith Cove, where the Impressionists painted. Rothko painted the Reed and Gamage wharfs from Banner Hill, and Gottlieb sketched them from a similar spot, possibly beside him. The hilltop is private; look from the road.

In the summer of 1934 Rothko and his wife, Edith Sachar, rented a house on Calder Street, about half a mile from the wharfs, while the Averys and the Gottliebs summered nearby. The Rothkos arrived first and took the house the Gottliebs had wanted. The house number is not recorded; this is a quiet residential street.
A harbor walk, then a short drive
Leonard Craske’s ⟦0⟧Man at the Wheel⟦1⟧, dedicated August 23, 1925. The plaques list 5,368 men known to have been lost at sea; a single storm in 1862 took 120 men, and storms in 1879 took 159.
At its peak Gorton’s ran dozens of wharves and many flake yards, where cod from the North Atlantic banks was split, salted and dried.
The harbor’s museum of its own working history, on the inner harbor.
The point where Lane painted Ten Pound Island and Hopper painted the fishermen’s houses of the Italian Quarter.
Rothko’s 1934 wharfs had fish flakes on the pier, the last generation of the racks Lane had painted eighty years before.
Low wooden racks on which split, salted cod was laid out in the sun to dry. Whole fields of them appear in Lane’s and later paintings of the waterfront.
Nets hung like a curtain in the water, catching fish by the gills. Mellen’s ⟦0⟧Gloucester Harbor (Laying Nets)⟦1⟧ shows crews setting them.

Small flat-bottomed boats carried on the schooners and rowed out to set lines and nets; Gordon Parks photographed Gloucester crews laying nets by hand from them in 1943. Homer drew boys in dories in 1873.
The fore-and-aft rigged vessels of the Gloucester fleet that brought fish home from the banks.
Lane a native, working there 1840s–1865; Mellen his student in the 1850s
Avery from 1921; Gottlieb and Rothko with him in the 1930s
